title: Why does everyone seem to use Unity for AI-assisted game development?
author: Illustrious_Exit_691
selftext:
Hey everyone!



I've been working on my game with Codex + UE5.4 for a few months now. Codex edits my Unreal project files directly, and I haven't set up any MCP tools or anything like that.



But whenever I look at Reddit or X, it feels like almost everyone using AI for game dev is working with Unity.



I'm a solo dev making a Singleplayer stylized 3D third-person game. It's more on the low-poly side, but I still want it to look good. I'm not going for realistic graphics.



So I'm wondering, is there a reason Unity seems to be more popular for AI-assisted development? Is it actually easier for AI agents to work with?



Would switching from Unreal to Unity be worth it at this point, or should I just stick with UE5 and maybe set up MCP?

comments.author: ziptofaf
comments.body:
Admittedly I don't really use that much of AI in game dev but I think I can answer this one, there are 2 reasons:

a) First is that Unity in GENERAL is more popular than Unreal (on PC I think it's about 2-3x difference, on mobiles Unity has like 90% of the market). UE5 hardware requirements alone scare away devs - you want it to actually run smoothly? Well, need an RTX capable card and preferably 64GB RAM. Compilation times are a problem too. It's also really opinionated - if you are making a third person 3D game then it's fantastic. If you want a 2D JRPG then it's garbage. Unreal really from the start was made with AA/AAA in mind. So by definition you will see more Unity than Unreal pretty much everywhere.

b) The biggest reason for single devs to use Unreal is blueprints. Except LLMs don't really like blueprints. It's a great system for non-programmers and game designers to program. But LLM can spit out C++ code directly without problems. Blueprints are harder to maintain.

And if you have few months of work already then switching an engine is probably not worth it. It's not a 1:1 conversion - assuming by 'few months' you mean daily and its few hundred hours of LLM work already then it would take a solid week to actually do it once you account for all the testing and edge cases. And learning the engine itself.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
UE is just as fine for AI to work with as Unity. The only downsides are:

1. High resource demands when editor is open, depending on the scene. But even if it's a fairly lightweight scene, the base demands are significantly higher than other engines. This makes it almost impossible to have multiple agents working on different engine tasks at the same time.

2. See #1. Also, any time you make a change that requires restarting the editor, it has the longest load time of any major engine and it's not particularly close. Compared to Godot which AI can launch and test 50x in 5 seconds.. it can slow development down.

In fact UE is the engine making the largest push towards AI support in the future, going so far as to retire Blueprints in order to push its language that's specifically designed for AI integration.

That being said, AI works just fine in the other major engines too. The real question is what you need from your engine. I use UE because I am heavily invested in the nanite technology. My entire game is based on abusing nanite to the fullest. I can have 100,000 clouds in the sky that are actual mesh and it adds about .1ms gpu processing time. But that's only because I gave up certain things in order to just go a full nanite processing pipeline. Prior to that I had been using Unity because i found it was the best overall balance for a game (and probably why so many people use it.) It finds a nice place between great C++ performance and feature parity and should probably be the go-to choice for a ny 3d project. I would've said Godot for full 2d if they weren't so against AI. And UE would've always been a, "If you need its tech." Because if you do, there really is no replacement for it. If they push AI integration to new levels later, maybe they'd become my goto over Unity as a base recommendation for 3d.

replies.author: DigitalDustChan
replies.body: Just curious: Unity has ECS/DOTS. In your view is that not a valid replacement for nanite?

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
They're very different. However, you've kind of hit something on the head that I might as well explain, because it helps underline why I think Unity is the best go-to 3d engine if you don't have specific Unreal needs:

So ECS/DOTS is incredible. It allows Unity to have \~2-3x as many actors as Unreal loaded on screen at once. However these are specifically full, physics enabled actors. You can have physics based hair, clothing, etc on these actors, morph targets on the faces, transparent meshes, etc. Godot isn't even in the running here, because in the benchmarks I saw, it could support like 1/10th of Unreal's, in the same simulation.

Now, that's full physics enabled actors. That means no nanite on them. And in fairness to Unreal, Unreal DOES handle smaller numbers smoother than Unity (and Godot actually handles very low numbers better than both, with minimal load for the  first handful).

These were not small numbers. I think Unity could push several hundred of the actors they were testing, and Unreal was like half t hat. This clearly shows with a traditional pipeline where you want to have physics enabled clothing, or hair, or transparent billboards, or whatever.. a standard pipeline where polys and LODs are kept tight, Unity actually wins out when using ECS/DOTS.

However, when they compared objects that did not have physics, Unity could push something like 1000\~ (might've been a bit more) before it reached the point of unplayability, and you saw performance decreases LONG before that (naturally). However Unreal doing the same thing but with nanite on meant they had perfect FPS even when they'd loaded 100,000 of the objects onto the screen. This is because nanite basically just converts everything into pixels. There are constraints to it still that have to be worked around (such as not using physics for your animations) and this is dependent upon the objects not being unique instances, too, but you could spawn 100,000 of the same 100 trees and the only real cost, outside of the flat pixel rendering and nanites calculation overhead is the VRAM cost for each of those 100 base meshes  (which can be significant if each object's polys are extremely high.). Still, it's crazy that you can simulate an entire forest with perfect density and it doesn't bother FPS at all.

However, the second you start mixing and matching non nanite meshes  (let's say you want some trees to have physics animations and others will just use world position or vertex animations), every one of those physics enabled meshes causes nanite redraws and overhead and suddenly you have an insanely laggy game.

Unity, however, let's you mix and match whatever the fuck you want. You just have to care about traditional game dev pipeline concerns like aggressive LOD use, smart topology, etc. Unreal throws a lot of these concepts out the window but makes you think about what you're adding to the game in a very different way.

Also, the various Unreal features related to that workflow all came out with Unreal 5, and have been spread amongst a number of updates. Information on how to work with it and its limitations is still hit or miss. One article will tell you nanite can't be used with skeletal meshes, another will note that it was added in \~5.5. So.. another reason why I wouldn't make it my default, go-to engine unless someone knows exactly what they're getting into. In which case it becomes a fucking amazing tool that can make games no other engine can (with tradeoffs, of course.) I'm also a big fan of metahumans within the Unreal ecosystem. The tools they've provided for indies on that front are great. Lumen is brilliant, but I hate working with realistic lighting so... less my cup of tea. Realistic lighting is just too demanding on performance, imo, even when it's highly optimized. Maybe some day they'll figure out how to make volumetric fog scale infinitely and I'll be sold on distant godrays.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: Mostly, yeah. The TL:DR is basically - nanite abstracts meshes. It takes all the visible polys on the screen and compresses them into this fuckery of pixel data so you still see the same image but the gpu isn't processing millions, billions, or even trillions of polys on the screen. It's kind of similar in concept to how textures are handled on a screen. More texture instances doesn't worsen performance, and texture size (2k vs 4k vs etc) doesn't create higher demand on the GPU by being on the screen (the only thing that matters is the space in the vram and potentially loading times). This is why trim sheets are so powerful.

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
I thought everyone was using Godot. Or Three.js. 

Most of my games have been in Three.js. But I have this massive asset library for Unity and Unreal I've built up over the years, and I wanted to use some of that easily. 

AI can work with Unity very well, arguably better than with Three.js, because so much is already known about Unity. It's been out for ages, there are many large forums where people have asked how to implement something in Unity and gotten many answers. Since the AI is trained on these very forums like StackOverflow and Unity forums, they know a lot about how to implement things. And the amount of documentation means the AI has an easy time gathering all the information it needs. 

The biggest problem with Three.js imo is that it provides so little. You have to write your entire game engine around it. There is less documentation, less examples, few ready to use components apart from rendering, and so you basically have to implement something similar to Unity, for every game you're making.

Consider also just level development. The AI was making all of my levels in hard to edit (for a human) JSON files. (A)I had to write a 3d planner like Unity's scene editor so I could do levels by hand. 

Unity gives you lots of documentation, forums full of questions and answers, a huge ecosystem of packages, the 3d editor, and all of the essentials for hand crafting your game. Unreal and Godot do a similar thing for their own ecosystems, and basically offer the same things. 

It's much less work for you and the AI to use a game development engine. So much of what you need has been worked out already and has a huge library of supporting software. If you don't use an engine, you have to do all of that yourself.
